analysis.title: Employment review: Payrolls surge with UE rate edging down. No serious signs of overheating.
key_insights: October payrolls rose 165k, well above MS estimate of 60k and consensus of 70k. Prior months were revised up a net 84k, which unwound the hints of softening in the prior report.
Private payrolls rose 159k (MS est 60k, consensus 65k), accelerating from averages of 126k over 3 months and 82k over 6 months. Quarterly private averages were 78k in 1Q, 79k in 2Q and 83k in 3Q.
The unemployment rate edged down to 4.1% (4.14% unrounded) from 4.18%. Labor force participation rose 0.1pt to 61.9%, and the unemployment rate would have fallen further without that rise.

The participation increase was centered among workers aged 55+ (36.9% to 37.2%) and 16-24 year-olds (56.3% to 56.4%). Prime-age participation was unchanged at 83.7%. MS notes the 55+ series is volatile and could easily reverse next month.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% m/m and 3.1% y/y. The prior month was revised up 0.2 to 3.2%, so the wage slowdown is less pronounced than previously reported.

The one soft element was hours worked. Production worker hours fell 0.2% m/m to begin the quarter and are up at a 0.5% annual rate versus 3Q, below the earlier 1% gains. MS says this suggests softer underlying labor demand than the headline data.
Aggregate private payroll income (payrolls x hours x AHE) began 4Q up at a 5.7% annual rate versus 3Q, after gains of about 4.0% in the prior two quarters.

The upside surprise versus MS estimates came from professional and business services (+70k vs a 10-20k monthly trend) and health and social services (+55k, which had been moderating). Transport and warehousing (+25k) was also strong.
Goods-related payrolls (manufacturing, retail, wholesale, transport) kept their recent pace in October but did not accelerate further.

Holiday hiring plans look strong: 300k tech hiring plans vs 250k a year ago, and 100k transport plans vs close to none last year. MS says part of this likely reflects higher online market share rather than extra strength, since retailer plans total 78k vs 112k last year.

MS expects the payroll breakeven pace (the pace consistent with a flat unemployment rate) at about 50k a month this year. The 3-month and 6-month averages have rebounded to near that level, and MS says the 12-month average exaggerates the slowdown. Payrolls can keep rising at around this year's pace, though not October's, without overly tightening the labor market.

MS says the report keeps the Fed on track for a December hike. Other labor indicators (lower jobless claims, a somewhat stronger JOLTS, strong Challenger holiday hiring plans, a solid ADP) are consistent with some tightening, but the unemployment rate decline does not point to too much of it.

Wage growth is decelerating mainly in services. Services AHE is 2.8% y/y vs 3.9% a year earlier, while goods AHE is 4.2% y/y and roughly sideways. The ECI suggests the services slowdown reflects compositional shifts in employment more than slower wage rates.

In the household survey, the employment-to-population ratio rose from 59.21% to 59.35%, the fourth consecutive monthly increase. The main driver was faster transitions from out of the labor force directly into employment.
After correcting for population-control distortions, MS finds no change in the participation rate between June 2025 and May 2026. October's 61.9% is a tenth above May's rate.

MS says rising inflation has cut into labor income purchasing power and forced households to use tax refunds and savings drawdowns to support spending. It expects disinflation to restore purchasing power over time, but slowly.

tension_points.bull_case: Payrolls of 165k beat consensus of 70k, the unemployment rate fell to 4.14%, the employment-to-population ratio rose for a fourth month, and claims, JOLTS, Challenger hiring plans and ADP all point to some tightening. That keeps the Fed on track for a December hike.
tension_points.bear_case: Production worker hours fell 0.2% m/m, which suggests softer underlying labor demand than the headline. The participation gain was concentrated in volatile 55+ workers and could reverse, and MS does not expect the October payroll pace to continue.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A reversal of the 55+ participation gain next month, or payrolls falling back toward the roughly 50k breakeven pace with hours worked staying weak.
